To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HTER is a good indicator of translation quality, and that it can be estimated with a good level of reliability from features that can be automatically extracted from the source and target sentences.

(1) HTER is a reliable indicator of post-editing effort; (2) the difficulty of translating a source sentence is a good predictor of post-editing time; and (3) HTER can be estimated using a number of features, some of which can be obtained from the translation system output.
(1) the quality of a translation is not homogeneous across segments and (2) it is possible to estimate post-editing effort in terms of HTER at the sentence level.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (i) how do translators post-edit MT systems?; (ii) what are the features that influence the post-editing effort?; (iii) can we estimate post-editing effort with a set of features?; and (iv) how do we use this information in the translation process?
the following questions: 1. How can we estimate translation post-edit effort at sentence level? 2. How can we use these estimates to filter out bad quality translations?
the problem of predicting the amount of post-editing effort needed to produce high quality translations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this work provides a novel approach to estimating the post-editing effort of machine translated sentences, which has a number of potential applications in the translation workflow.
our approach to estimate post-editing effort is a good starting point for a translation workflow, but that further work is required to improve it.
HTER is a reliable and simple metric for estimating post-editing effort, which can be obtained from the translation workflow.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proposed method is able to identify the sentences that are likely to need more effort in the post-editing process, and that this information can be used to improve translation quality.

we have developed an approach to predict translation effort at the sentence level based on the source sentence, the translation and a set of features that can be automatically obtained from the translation workflow.
HTER can be a good candidate to filter out bad quality translations and therefore improve the productivity of postediting MT systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the translation post-editing process can be made more efficient by estimating post-editing effort for each sentence.
the translation industry needs to have more reliable metrics for filtering MT output and that the development of these metrics should be a priority in the MT research agenda.

the difficulty of a source sentence can be estimated from features such as its length or the number of words in the source sentence, while the quality of the translation can be assessed from the number of edits required by the post-editor to produce the final translation.
